extra.message: Unauthenticated API user deletion (Broken Function Level Authorization) — Complete account takeover and denial of service; any user including admins can be deleted without credentials. [verified: Same as finding [2]: @token_required commented out on /api/v1/delete-user/<user_id> (line 221) with no fallback auth in delete(), enabling unauthenticated account deletion.]

Missing authentication and authorization on user deletion API endpoint — Unauthenticated attackers can delete any user account including administrators, causing denial of service and data loss. [verified: DELETE /api/v1/delete-user/<user_id> has @token_required commented out at line 221 and delete() contains no authentication or authorization check, letting any unauthenticated attacker delete arbitrary user accounts.]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via unvalidated picture_url — Attacker can scan internal networks, access cloud metadata services, hit internal admin endpoints, or use the server as a proxy. [verified: POST /api/v1/update_picture takes picture_url from the JSON body and passes it directly to requests.get() with no URL validation, allowlisting, or sanitization, and the endpoint has no authentication (no @token_required, no session check).]

Hardcoded weak SECRET_KEY enabling session and JWT forgery — Attackers can forge session cookies to impersonate any user (including admins) and forge valid JWT tokens for API access, completely bypassing authentication. [verified: SECRET_KEY='just_another_secret' is hardcoded at config.py:7, loaded into Flask via app.config.from_object(Config) in __init__.py:10, and used for both Flask session signing and JWT encode/decode at api_v1.py:94,133. No external override, rotation, or environment-variable fallback exists.]

SQL Injection in dashboard file search — Attacker can read, modify, or delete arbitrary data from the SQLite database including all users' credentials and files. [verified: search_query from request.args is interpolated directly into f-string SQL on line 137 with no parameterization, sanitization, or escaping; user_id is session-derived but search_query is fully attacker-controlled.]

Mass assignment enabling privilege escalation via role/permissions — Any authenticated user can set their own role to admin and permissions to all, gaining full administrative access to the application. [verified: Same as findings 4 and 12: lines 188-196 accept role/permissions from request.form with only a key-presence check and no admin authorization, enabling self-privilege-escalation to admin.]

Mass assignment leading to privilege escalation via role/permissions fields — Any authenticated user can self-assign the admin role and full permissions, gaining complete control over the application. [verified: Same as finding 4: the web update_profile route on lines 188-196 applies no admin authorization check on role/permissions fields from request.form, allowing any authenticated user to self-assign admin privileges.]

Path traversal in file upload — Arbitrary file write anywhere the Flask process has write permission; can overwrite Python source files, templates, or create executable files for RCE. [verified: Same as finding 2: file.filename is used unsanitized in os.path.join on line 264 and file.save on line 265 with no secure_filename() or path validation, enabling arbitrary file write.]

Unauthenticated API profile data access (Broken Function Level Authorization) — Mass disclosure of user PII, credentials context, roles, and permissions to unauthenticated attackers. [verified: Same as finding [1]: @token_required commented out on /api/v1/profile (line 152) with no auth check in get(), exposing all users' profiles to unauthenticated access.]

Missing authentication on API update_picture endpoint — Unauthenticated attacker can trigger SSRF against internal services and arbitrarily modify any user's profile picture record. [verified: Same as finding [3]: POST /api/v1/update_picture post() at line 243 has neither @token_required nor session authentication, leaving it fully exposed.]

Insecure session cookie configuration — HttpOnly disabled, no Secure/SameSite — Session cookies are accessible via JavaScript (exacerbating XSS impact), transmitted over unencrypted HTTP, and vulnerable to CSRF attacks. [verified: SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=False is set at config.py:6 and applied in run.py:9; no SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE or SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE is set anywhere in the codebase, leaving session cookies readable by JavaScript and transmittable over unencrypted HTTP.]

DEBUG mode enabled exposing interactive debugger and stack traces — Attackers can trigger errors to view sensitive configuration, source code, and environment variables, and may achieve remote code execution via the Werkzeug debugger console if accessible. [verified: DEBUG=True at config.py:5 is loaded via from_object and passed to app.run(debug=debug_mode) at run.py:7,10, enabling the Werkzeug interactive debugger with stack traces, source disclosure, and potential PIN-protected RCE console.]

Insecure cookie configuration — HttpOnly disabled, missing Secure and SameSite flags — Session cookie accessible to JavaScript; XSS can directly exfiltrate session tokens for account takeover. Cookie also transmitted over unencrypted HTTP and vulnerable to CSRF. [verified: SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=False at config.py:6 and absence of Secure/SameSite flags confirmed by codebase search; same misconfiguration as finding 1, enabling cookie theft via any XSS vector present elsewhere.]

Unrestricted file upload with no type or content validation — Upload of malicious scripts, web shells, or malware; combined with path traversal leads to arbitrary file write and potential RCE. [verified: Same as finding 3: no file-type, extension, or content validation on upload; files are saved with original attacker-supplied names directly to a web-accessible directory.]

IDOR via user_id in API profile endpoint — Cross-user data access; any authenticated API client can enumerate and retrieve all user profiles including roles, permissions, and PII. [verified: Even if @token_required were re-enabled, the profile endpoint takes user_id from query args and returns profile data without ever checking whether the authenticated current_user is authorized to view that specific user_id.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints — Attackers can perform unlimited brute-force password guessing against user accounts and automated mass account creation for spam or resource exhaustion. [verified: No rate limiting, lockout, or throttling is present on the login route (line 21) or signup route; unlimited brute-force and automated account creation are possible.]

User enumeration via signup error message — Attacker can compile a list of existing usernames/emails for targeted credential-stuffing or phishing attacks. [verified: Same as findings 7 and 16: the signup IntegrityError handler on line 103 returns a response distinguishable from a successful registration, enabling username/email enumeration.]

User enumeration via signup error message — Attackers can build a list of valid usernames for targeted password spraying or phishing attacks. [verified: Same as finding 7: the signup route on line 103 returns a distinguishable error on duplicate username/email vs. a redirect on success, enabling reliable account enumeration.]

Missing CSRF protection on all state-changing routes — Attackers can perform unauthorized actions (file upload/delete, profile modification, privilege escalation) on behalf of authenticated users via cross-site request forgery. [verified: No CSRF tokens exist on any state-changing POST route (upload, delete, update_profile, login, signup); Flask has no built-in CSRF protection and no Flask-WTF or manual token mechanism is implemented.]

Missing CSRF protection on state-changing endpoints — Attacker can craft malicious pages that force authenticated users to unknowingly delete files, upload content, or modify their profile (including privilege escalation via mass assignment). [verified: Same as findings 6 and 15: no CSRF tokens exist on any state-changing POST route; Flask's default behavior lacks CSRF protection and no compensating control is present.]

Missing CSRF protection on all state-changing routes — Attackers can perform unauthorized actions (file upload, profile modification, file deletion) on behalf of authenticated victims via cross-site request forgery. [verified: Same as finding 6: no CSRF tokens are present on any state-changing POST routes; no Flask-WTF or manual CSRF validation is implemented anywhere in the application.]

Missing authentication on profile picture serving — Unauthenticated access to all user profile pictures; information disclosure via predictable sequential filenames. [verified: The /uploads/profile_pictures/<filename> route on line 307 has no session check or @login_required decorator; any unauthenticated user can access any user's profile picture by guessing sequential numeric filenames.]

Path traversal in file delete — Arbitrary file deletion of files that the attacker previously wrote via the upload path traversal vulnerability. [verified: Same as finding 1: the delete route joins unsanitized filename into file_path on line 342 and calls os.remove on line 363; the DB ownership check does not prevent path traversal when a traversal-named file exists in the database.]

Path traversal via arbitrary file delete with unsanitized filename — Attacker who can upload a file with a traversal name can later delete arbitrary files on the server filesystem accessible to the process. [verified: filename from URL path is joined unsanitized into file_path on line 342 and passed to os.remove on line 362; the DB ownership check on line 355 uses a parameterized query but does not validate the path, so an attacker who first uploads a traversal-named file (via finding 2) can delete arbitrary filesystem targets.]

Weak MD5 password hashing with no salt — Password hashes can be cracked near-instantly via rainbow tables or brute force if the database is exposed; complete compromise of all user accounts. [verified: Same as finding 5: custom_hash uses unsalted single-round MD5—cryptographically broken and trivial to crack with rainbow tables if the password database is exposed.]
